overview: Two pollination strategies in flowering plants, differing in whether pollen comes from the same flower/plant or a different one.
genZNote: Self-pollination: keeping it in the family. Cross-pollination: bringing in fresh genetic material from outside.

aspects.label: Source of Pollen
aspects.valueA: Pollen from the same flower or a genetically identical flower on the same plant.
aspects.valueB: Pollen from a flower on a genetically different plant of the same species.

aspects.label: Genetic Variation Produced
aspects.valueA: Little to no new genetic variation; tends to increase homozygosity.
aspects.valueB: Introduces new genetic combinations, increasing variation and often vigour.

aspects.label: Requires External Agent?
aspects.valueA: Does not require an external pollinating agent.
aspects.valueB: Usually requires agents like wind, water, insects, or birds.

aspects.label: Example
aspects.valueA: Pea plants (Mendel's chosen organism, mostly self-pollinating).
aspects.valueB: Most flowering plants relying on insect or wind pollination.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Mendel deliberately chose the pea plant partly because it naturally self-pollinates, which made controlling his crosses much easier.
overlay.memoryTrick: Self = same flower/plant. Cross = crosses over to a different plant.
overlay.commonMisconception: Self-pollination is not automatically 'inferior' — it guarantees seed production even without pollinators, which is a major reproductive advantage in some environments.
